Operon-S1
System 1 ⋅\cdot fast decisions
 

Operon-S1:
a fast decision controller for long-horizon biomedical agents

 

Genoria AI Team

Yuejie Hou, Yueyuxiao Yang, Weiting Tang, Meng Yang

Genoria AI

29 October 2026

Abstract

Language-model agents now carry out long scientific work in biology, but their judgements about conventions, skills, errors, evidence and stopping are made inside the reasoning that does the work, where they cannot be measured, replaced or improved on their own. Here we present Operon-S1, a fast decision system, a System 1 for the agent, that separates judging from doing. A decision harness poses the agent’s recurring judgements as closed questions at 13 decision points and acts only through fixed messages that never contain an answer, so any model that answers the questions can serve as the judge. Across seven life-science benchmarks, a local decision model took over these judgements in 0.6 s at the median for an in-loop request on CPU at no request cost, with no measurable change in the agent’s score on five of six benchmarks, whereas the general language model that drives the agent, asked the same questions, accounted for 8.0% to 35.2% of task cost. Every decision is recorded with its consequence. Retraining on labels from task construction, verifiers or execution raised decision accuracy on every question in each of three trained versions, and a new version enters service only through a promotion gate. Task-level results in this study use the public checkpoint. The same closed decisions serve wet-laboratory protocol troubleshooting and the design of a germline target enrichment panel. Like the regulator of an operon, which switches genes on and off without making their products, Operon-S1 steers the agent without doing its work, and makes the agent’s judgements a layer that can be measured, replaced and trained.

Introduction

Language-model agents now retrieve data, write and run analysis code, and translate scientific intent into executable laboratory procedures, in biology and biomedicine1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, where a general-purpose biomedical agent now carries out research tasks autonomously2, and in chemistry7. As these tasks lengthen, the limit on an agent shifts from what it can compute to how it judges its own work. A single analysis spans tens of steps, and along the way the agent meets questions that no tool answers: which convention a loosely worded task implies, which skill or file applies, what a failed command means, whether a value it has computed already answers the question, whether a slow computation should continue or yield its best result and, in laboratory work, which step of a protocol caused a failure. In such agents these judgements share one model’s reasoning with the computation, so none of them is posed, measured or corrected on its own.

These judgements carry scientific weight. The independent-filtering threshold of a differential-expression analysis changes which genes are reported8, a skill whose convention differs from the task’s can turn a correct analysis into a wrong answer, a misattributed protocol step sends the repeat experiment in the wrong direction, and a probe design judged by its design coverage alone can leave targets uncaptured. Once agents drive instruments, a misjudgement costs reagents and instrument time as well as compute. Reasoning agents can also favour extended internal reasoning over interacting with their environment, a failure termed overthinking9, and reasoning models keep deliberating after they have reached a correct answer10. In both cases more computation does not supply the missing judgement.

Cognitive science describes reasoning as the interplay of a fast, intuitive process and a slow, deliberate one11, 12, and it separates metacognitive monitoring, the assessment of one’s own progress, from metacognitive control, the decision to continue, change strategy or stop13. Fast decision models, sometimes called System-One models, map a short state and a closed question to a distribution over a fixed set of options in a single forward pass14, 15, 16. Related approaches route queries between cheap and expensive models17, 18, 19, learn when to defer to a downstream decision maker20 or score intermediate steps with learned verifiers21, 22 and process reward models23, 24. Language models also act as judges of other models’ outputs25, 26 and as critics that flag errors in code27, and their verdicts are free text written by a model. Selective prediction, abstaining when uncertain, is the classical way to contain a fast model’s errors28, 29, and conformal prediction gives such abstention distribution-free guarantees30, 31. In agent pipelines, System-One models have reduced calls to large models without loss of task success32, supported scientific decisions over prepared evidence33, scored the recurring decisions of search agents34 and answered typed questions over clinical records35.

The same work also marks the limits of this approach. For a decision model fine-tuned on a browser agent’s model-labelled decisions, held-out decision agreement rose from 19% to 75% without a corresponding gain in task success36, savings shrank once the cost of the decision model was counted16, and an open-weight local decision model changed 30% of its answers when the option order was reversed16. In a cascade between a fast verifier and a large model, a matched random-escalation control showed that the savings came from how much was escalated rather than from the fast model’s probabilities37. Scientific agents raise three further problems. The decisions that matter are scientific: conventions, analysis routes and whether the evidence suffices. A decision can sit tens of steps before the score it affects, because only the final answer is scored. And a fast model meant to improve as the agent works needs evidence of improvement from outside its own training loop.

An agent can hold its judgements in three ways, distinguished by two criteria: whether each judgement is posed on its own, and whether the model that answers it is trained and replaced against labels that no model produces. In the first, the judgements stay inside the reasoning of the model that does the work, and they change only when that model, its prompt or its skills change. In the second, judgements are lifted out to a fast model, one at a time17, 20, 21 or several at once34, 35, and the model is judged by cost, by task success or against labels from people or language models. In the third, every recurring judgement of the run is posed as a closed question with a verifiable label, and the model that answers is replaced only under a gate. Operon-S1 takes the third route: it separates judging from doing.

Self-improving agents have refined their behaviour through verbal reflection on failures38 and iterative self-feedback39, accumulated libraries of reusable skills40, rewritten their own code41, 42 and evolved programs under automated evaluators43. In these systems a change is kept when it improves the signal that drives the search. A controller for scientific judgements needs a stricter test, because its labels are imbalanced and a candidate can score well by learning only the most frequent answer. Operon-S1 therefore keeps a new version only if it beats its parent and three baselines on labels that no model produces. Statistical adoption gates can control false adoptions in adaptive model search44, and no automated gate can in general both refuse every bad update and accept every good one45, so the gate here gives its guarantees only on a bounded, labelled split.

Here we introduce Operon-S1, a fast decision controller for long-horizon biomedical agents, paired with the ProtoPilot agent1 (Fig. 1). As an external model, it takes over the two functions that metacognition research separates, monitoring and control13. The name refers to the operon46, in which a regulatory protein switches a cluster of genes on or off without making their products, as the controller regulates the agent’s work without doing it, and “S1” to the fast process, System 1, of dual-process accounts of reasoning11. ProtoPilot coordinates protocol, computational and coding agents, verifies each stage against expert-grounded rubrics, and has generated standard operating procedures and instrument code that pass device-level validity checks across four laboratory automation platforms1.

Operon-S1 adds a decision layer with three parts to the agent, and ProtoPilot is the agent with which it is tested here. The decision harness is preset for each domain and triggers autonomously. It builds each state deterministically from the facts of the run, so the agent never assembles the context and every decision can be replayed, and it poses closed questions at 13 decision points from the start of a task to the submission of its answer (Table 1). The fast decision model answers each question with a probability for each option and acts through four fixed actions: brief, remind, end the tool loop or request one recheck. The local decision model, LAYA, runs on CPU. A hosted model, JEV, serves as a comparator, and a second comparator places a general language model in the same harness. LAYA is retrained in gated rounds on decisions from a data-synthesis pipeline. With the harness, the questions and the messages fixed, the system is designed to change only the decision model during retraining, so each change in behaviour can be attributed to it.

Each design choice follows from a property of the science. Because a judgement can decide a score without changing the computation, a message may name a convention, a file or a quantity to verify but never an answer value. Because conventions, evidence, error classes and answer formats can be checked by construction, verifiers or execution, each judgement is a closed question whose answer can be compared with such a label.

We find that this layer can be measured, replaced and traced at little cost. Six controllers, from rules to a general language model, ran on the same states, questions and messages, and in the 2,361 runs whose answers can be matched as text no injected message contained the gold answer. The local decision model answered single in-loop requests in under a second at the median and accounted for 0.8% to 5.2% of wall-clock time at no request cost. With its public checkpoint as the judge, the decision layer lowered cost on SeqQA by 5.8% and agent steps on protocolqa2 by 10.3%, with no measurable score change on five of six benchmarks. On seqqa2, every acting controller lowered the score, the local model least. Training on verifiable labels raised accuracy over the public checkpoint on every decision question in each of three trained versions, analysis family from 0.26 to 0.99 in the first. The gains carried over to the agent’s own decision states on held-out benchmark items, where analysis-family accuracy rose from 0.056 to 1.000 and execution-labelled error-class accuracy from 0.174 to 0.408. The same closed decisions extend to laboratory-protocol troubleshooting, where the errors are of diagnosis rather than of routing, and to probe design, where a fall in panel coverage from 88% to 16% traces to three causes, each answered by one closed design action.

Results

Operon-S1 lifts the agent’s judgements into a separate decision layer

Operon-S1 separates judging from doing. The judgements of the agent go to a separate fast decision model through the decision harness, and all doing stays with the agent (Fig. 1a). The slow system is the ProtoPilot agent1, here driven by DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at high reasoning effort, which plans, writes and runs code in a sandbox and composes the answer. The harness layer triggers autonomously during the run, reads its facts and poses closed questions. These cover the analysis family, the expected answer type, relevant files and candidate skills, and conventions that the task implies but does not state. They also ask whether the evidence already answers the task, whether a long computation should stop with its best result, which class an error belongs to, whether the code follows the required convention, and whether the answer meets its format and conventions (Table 1). In the terms of Nelson and Narens13, the answers to these questions are the controller’s monitoring of the agent’s progress, and the actions they trigger are its control.

The controller answers each question with a probability distribution over its options and acts only when it is confident, abstaining otherwise as in selective prediction28. Its actions are to brief the agent, remind it, end the tool loop with a final-answer instruction or request one recheck, each delivered through a message written in advance that may name a convention, a file or a quantity to verify. All controllers share this policy and these messages and differ only in the distributions they return, with one exception for the rule-based controller (Methods), so a comparison between controllers is a comparison between their judgements. Throughout, “controller” denotes any policy in the controller slot, including the no-op and rule-based controls, and “fast decision model” denotes the learned or hosted model behind it.

A no-op controller renders and records every state but always abstains, and leaves the agent’s model requests unchanged (Methods). The effect of a controller ϕ\phi on a task outcome YY is the contrast

Δϕ=𝔼⁡[Y⁡(ϕ)]−𝔼⁡[Y⁡(ϕ0)],\Delta_{\phi}=\mathbb{E}\bigl[Y(\phi)\bigr]-\mathbb{E}\bigl[Y(\phi_{0})\bigr], (1)

where ϕ0\phi_{0} is the no-op controller and the expectation is over tasks and runs; the controller’s own latency is charged against each task’s time limit. The evaluation has seven arms. The baseline is the original agent without the harness. The other six run the same harness with different controllers (Fig. 1b):

  • •

    the no-op control;

  • •

    a rule-based controller that uses lexical matching, error-message patterns and budget fractions;

  • •

    a self-verification control that requests a recheck whenever the answer check would pose a question;

  • •

    JEV, a hosted System-One model14, used as a comparator;

  • •

    LAYA, a local 322-million-parameter encoder47 served on CPU, whose public checkpoint is version 0 of the trained controller;

  • •

    a general-LLM controller, in which DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash answers the same closed questions in the same harness, with the same states, policy and messages.

The general-LLM arm measures what a fast decision model adds over asking a general language model the same questions. In every batch of the main table, JEV, LAYA and the general-LLM controller have equal time budgets for each request (Methods).

For every decision we keep a provenance record of the distribution, the action, whether the agent adopted it and the task outcome (Fig. 1a), which links a decision to a score assigned only to the final answer.

Judgements rather than computation decided most of the original agent’s lost items and surplus time

The judgements that the layer poses are where the original agent lost items and time. Most wrong answers of the original ProtoPilot agent on BixBench-Verified-50 arose from a judgement after the computation. The agent answered 12 of the 49 gradable items wrongly (Methods). On 5, the correct value was already in its output under another convention. On 1 it misread the direction of an effect, and on 2 it broke the required answer format. On 3 it lacked an offline resource, and on 1 none of its computed variants matched the reference. The first three groups, 8 of 12, turned on a choice made after the computation, where a controller can act. A further judgement, when to stop, costs mainly time, measured directly as the wall-clock time after the answer first appeared (Fig. 2a). For each task with a locatable answer we recorded the answer time t∗t^{\ast}, the first moment at which the value the agent finally submitted appeared in its own tool output, and measured the post-answer fraction of wall-clock time

ω=∑i∈I(Ti−ti∗)∑i∈ITi,\omega=\frac{\sum_{i\in I}\bigl(T_{i}-t_{i}^{\ast}\bigr)}{\sum_{i\in I}T_{i}}, (2)

where TiT_{i} is the wall-clock time of task ii and II the set of tasks with a locatable answer (Methods). On the 15 BixBench-Verified-50 tasks with a locatable answer, ω=0.47\omega=0.47: 1,798 of 3,860 s elapsed after the answer was already in the agent’s tool output. On SciAgentArena, where t∗t^{\ast} is taken as the first successful run of the solution script, 30% of all wall-clock time on the benchmark followed t∗t^{\ast} (14,709 of 48,852 s), and on seqqa2 16%; because tasks without a located t∗t^{\ast} add only to the denominator, these shares are lower bounds on ω\omega (Methods). Because timed-out tasks score zero, continuing can also cost the whole item. On seqqa2, four of five timed-out codon-optimization tasks had produced a valid candidate 69–353 s into a run that then continued to the limit.

The convention errors share a pattern. On each of the 5 items, the reference value or the reference convention had already appeared in the agent’s own output, but the agent submitted a value computed under another convention (Fig. 2b). In one case it ran a differential-expression analysis with the default independent-filtering threshold48, which reproduced the reference, and then reported the result of a different threshold. The difference between a right and a wrong answer was the choice between the default threshold of 0.1 and a threshold of 0.05.

Skill selection and error triage cost fewer items than conventions. Across 210 judged trajectories, loading a matching skill cost an item three times, because the skill text was wrong or its convention differed from the benchmark’s, whereas skipping one cost an item once (Fig. 2c). On BixBench-Verified-50, SciAgentArena and BiomniBench-DA, the agent recovered unaided from 82–94% of tool-error episodes, and the median error run lasted one call. Headroom therefore differs from one judgement to the next, which is why the layer poses, measures and trains each judgement on its own rather than repairing one failure class at a time.

The same analysis was applied to the baseline rounds of the formal evaluation, which used later skill releases and a higher reasoning effort (Methods; Extended Data Fig. 1). Of 121 wrong answers on the four benchmarks scored per item (SeqQA, seqqa2, BixBench-Verified-50 and SciAgentArena), a rule codebook assigned 9 to conventions, which it detects only where an answer matcher exists, 7 to stopping at the time limit and 1 to answer format. On 10 of 27 wrong answers with an automatic gold matcher, the correct value had already appeared in the agent’s own output. On tasks with a locatable answer, the post-answer fraction ω\omega was 0.33 on BixBench-Verified-50, 0.35 on SciAgentArena and 0.49 on seqqa2 (Extended Data Fig. 1).

The local decision model costs little beside the work it judges

A separate judge pays off only if it costs little beside the work it judges and leaves the agent unchanged when it abstains. We evaluated on seven benchmarks spanning sequence reasoning, laboratory-protocol troubleshooting, end-to-end data analysis and multi-step omics studies, 1,417 tasks in total (Table 2): LAB-Bench SeqQA49, LAB-Bench 2 seqqa2 and protocolqa250, BixBench-Verified-5051, 52, SciAgentArena53, BiomniBench-DA54, 55 and the public split of OmicsBench56. Each benchmark ran under its official prompt, network policy and primary metric, with every task in a fresh sandbox. The original agent was scheduled for five rounds to estimate between-round variation, and Extended Data Table 2 gives the number of rounds that completed on each benchmark (Methods). Paired changes in time, steps and accuracy against the baseline are shown in Fig. 3a,b and Extended Data Table 2. The hypotheses are that the controller reduces cost at non-inferior accuracy (H1) and that its gains exceed those of an extra recheck (H2). H1 is judged on five benchmarks, 1,289 tasks: SeqQA, seqqa2, BixBench-Verified-50, SciAgentArena and BiomniBench-DA. H2 is judged on SeqQA and seqqa2. OmicsBench, on which the controllers are inert, is run in the baseline arm only. protocolqa2 was added to the evaluation after the hypotheses were written, so its results are reported as exploratory.

The no-op control checks that the harness itself leaves the agent unchanged. Against the baseline, the no-op arm changed the official score by −0.030 to +0.014 and wall-clock time by −6.9% to +40.5%, and every 95% interval of its score, time and step changes included zero on the six benchmarks with paired tasks except the wall-clock change on BiomniBench-DA (+40.5% [+18.0, +66.4]), where its batches ran partly at a different concurrency (Methods) (Extended Data Table 3). An audit of the 16,042 messages injected in 5,743 task runs found no message that contained the gold answer in any of the 2,361 runs whose answers can be matched as text. The remaining 3,382 runs have free-text, file or sequence-design answers that cannot be matched automatically.

Relative to the baseline, the decision layer with LAYA version 0 as judge lowered cost on SeqQA by 5.8% [0.6, 10.8] at no request cost of its own; per task, JEV requests cost 0.19 to 0.48 thousandths of a dollar and general-LLM requests 2.1 to 9.8. On SciAgentArena the steps and cost of this arm changed by −6.8% [−18.6, +3.8] and −4.7% [−17.2, +7.6]. Its wall-clock change ranged from −14.0% to +2.6% across the hypothesis benchmarks, and its only score change with an interval excluding zero was −0.013 [−0.028, −0.001] on seqqa2 (Fig. 3a,b; Extended Data Table 2). JEV changed wall-clock time by −9.8% to +6.9% and steps by −6.2% to +4.0%, and lowered the seqqa2 score by 0.038 [0.018, 0.060]. The general-LLM controller changed wall-clock time by −5.2% to +16.2%, changed cost by −4.4% to +61.5%, and lowered the seqqa2 score by 0.048 [0.025, 0.072]. The rule-based controller reduced steps on SciAgentArena by 9.8% [1.2, 19.3] and on seqqa2 by 5.5% [0.9, 9.8], where its score fell by 0.018 [0.003, 0.035]. H1 requires an efficiency gain on at least four of the five hypothesis benchmarks and non-inferiority on every benchmark with a verdict (SciAgentArena, with one reference round, has none), and at the data cutoff it holds for no arm: the efficiency condition held on at most two benchmarks. Non-inferiority is limited by precision on two benchmarks. On BixBench-Verified-50 the score interval of the no-op control itself (−0.030 [−0.092, +0.023]) extended below the margin of 0.028, because 50 tasks in 33 clusters give an interval wider than the margin, and on SeqQA the margin is 0.0023, because two baseline rounds that agree closely give a between-round standard deviation of 0.001 (Methods).

On protocolqa2, an exploratory benchmark, LAYA version 0 and the general-LLM controller reduced steps by 10.3% [4.9, 15.7] and 10.9% [4.8, 16.8] with score changes of −0.008 and 0.000, and JEV changed the score by +0.032 [−0.024, +0.088]. On BiomniBench-DA, with all 50 tasks paired, JEV, LAYA version 0 and the general-LLM controller reduced steps by 16.6% [9.1, 23.2], 13.9% [5.9, 21.2] and 16.1% [9.5, 22.3] with no score change outside its interval, and the changes of JEV and LAYA are for reference only, because their batches ran at a different concurrency (Methods).

These figures include the controller’s own requests, latency and cost. In offline replay of 8,265 gate rows, the local controller answered in 266 ms at the median and 581 ms at the 95th percentile on CPU. During the evaluation, the median error-triage request (P3) took 576 ms for LAYA, 222 ms for JEV and 1,462 ms for the general-LLM controller, against 8 to 34 s for a slow-system step across benchmarks. The brief issues two sequential requests over the longest states. It took 7.3 s at the median on the local model, against a median of 164 s for a whole SeqQA task. The brief carries 7 to 31 questions and its requests queue on four shared replicas, whereas single in-loop requests took 0.5 to 0.8 s at the median (workspace bounds 531 ms, error triage 576 ms, answer check 667 ms, convention in code 811 ms, long computation 839 ms). Efficiency is reported per benchmark. Across benchmarks, the controller accounted for 0.3% to 1.4% of wall-clock time and 0.4% to 2.2% of cost per task for JEV, and for 1.9% to 16.9% and 8.0% to 35.2% for the general-LLM controller (Extended Data Fig. 2). LAYA version 0 accounted for 0.8% to 5.2% of wall-clock time and no request cost.

Provenance records separate whether a judgement is right, whether the agent acts on it and whether the task succeeds

Monitoring and control are measured separately. Monitoring quality is the agreement of each judgement with its label, by per-question accuracy and calibration (Extended Data Fig. 3; Extended Data Table 6). On benchmark states with execution- or benchmark-derived labels (error class, analysis family and answer type), per-question accuracy ranged from 0.865 to 1.000 for JEV and from 0.855 to 0.998 for the general-LLM controller, with expected calibration errors of 0.013 to 0.039 and 0.033 to 0.045. Version 0 of LAYA, the public checkpoint used zero-shot, was poorly matched to these states: 0.164 on error class (expected calibration error 0.360), 0.087 on analysis family and 0.663 on answer type, against 0.994 on answer format, where JEV scored 0.680 and the general-LLM controller 0.903 (Extended Data Table 6). Round 1 trains these questions on curriculum states. At the action threshold of 0.6, on error triage, JEV answered 91.2% of questions with an accuracy of 0.911 on those answered, and the general-LLM controller answered 92.9% with an accuracy of 0.882 (Extended Data Fig. 3). Control is measured by the contrast of equation (1), together with the post-answer fraction ω\omega of each arm (Fig. 3d). In the baseline ω\omega was 0.49 on SeqQA, 0.49 on seqqa2, 0.33 on BixBench-Verified-50 and 0.35 on SciAgentArena. Three arms changed it with an interval excluding zero: the general-LLM controller raised it on seqqa2 by 0.081 [0.036, 0.127], and the rule-based and self-verification controls lowered it on SciAgentArena by 0.044 [0.001, 0.092] and 0.061 [0.016, 0.123].

The self-verification control isolates the value of looking again before the answer is submitted. It uses the same states, triggers and messages as the learned controllers but requests a recheck whenever the answer check would pose a question. On SeqQA and seqqa2, JEV differed from the self-verification control by +0.002 [−0.010, +0.013] and −0.020 [−0.043, +0.003] in accuracy, at 6.5% and 10.2% higher cost. H2 is therefore not supported for JEV. LAYA version 0 and the general-LLM controller differed from the self-verification control by +0.005 and +0.005, and by +0.007 and −0.030, in accuracy on SeqQA and seqqa2, with every interval including zero, an exploratory comparison.

Against the baseline, on SeqQA, seqqa2, BixBench-Verified-50 and SciAgentArena together, LAYA version 0 turned 13 wrong answers right and 21 right answers wrong. JEV did so for 15 and 38 answers, and the general-LLM controller for 16 and 40 (exact McNemar test57 with Holm correction across benchmarks; Extended Data Table 4). Among the McNemar tests, after Holm correction the seqqa2 losses of the rule-based controller (0 gained, 12 lost, P = 0.002), the self-verification control (2 gained, 14 lost, P = 0.021), JEV (1 gained, 21 lost, P < 0.001), LAYA version 0 (0 gained, 10 lost, P = 0.010) and the general-LLM controller (1 gained, 25 lost, P < 0.001) remained significant, and no other test did. The seqqa2 losses of JEV and the general-LLM controller were concentrated in the synonymous-mutation and molecular-weight families, and changes fell on items of medium and high baseline difficulty (Extended Data Fig. 4). Because the loss is visible decision by decision, it can be located. On the 23 development items on which JEV lost answers that the baseline got right, the agent loaded the convention skill in 13 runs under JEV against 16 in the baseline.

The provenance records locate where effects arise (Fig. 3c). For each decision point we report how often it fired, how often the controller acted, how often the agent adopted the action and the outcome difference between adopted and non-adopted cases, a descriptive quantity because adoption is not randomized. The brief fired on every task, and the agent loaded a suggested skill after 38% of briefs under JEV and 7% under LAYA version 0. The answer check requested a recheck on 8.0% of its firings under JEV. The evidence check fired on at most one task per benchmark, and the long-computation check acted on 33% of its firings under the rule-based controller and 14% under the general-LLM controller on SciAgentArena. Workspace-bounds and convention-in-code reminders were adopted in 82% to 100% of cases (Fig. 3c).

Gated retraining couples a data-synthesis pipeline with a promotion gate

LAYA is retrained in gated rounds (Fig. 1c, Fig. 4a). Each round runs the data-synthesis pipeline, which turns an executable curriculum into decisions with verifiable labels, mines hard examples from the parent version’s errors, trains a candidate, fits a temperature-scaling calibration58 for it, and tests it against a promotion gate. A promoted version controls the agent and is the parent whose errors the next round mines, so each round starts from the last promoted version.

Round 1 draws its decisions from a synthetic curriculum of 1,517 executable bioinformatics tasks in 25 families, each with two independent implementations, metamorphic checks59 and a verifier that accepts its reference answer and rejects constructed negatives. Four generators turn these tasks into decisions with the controller’s own state renderer and questions, so that training states have the form of deployment states (Extended Data Table 1). Labels come only from construction, a verifier or code execution. This follows programmatic supervision60 but needs no label model, because these labels are exact. A fault example is kept only if running it fails. Round 1 builds every decision from templates. A leakage firewall admits only rows with these label sources, no lineage through the comparator and no overlap with the benchmarks’ task text61, 62 (Methods).

A loss-weighted variant of hard-example mining63 samples rows within each question with a weight that increases with the parent version’s loss and doubles for confident errors. Each candidate is paired with a random-subset control trained on the same number of rows per question, which gives the gate a baseline of equal training budget. Let 𝒬∗\mathcal{Q}^{\ast} be the questions with headroom, on which the rule-based controller scores at most 0.95. A candidate θ′\theta^{\prime} replaces its parent θ\theta only if 𝒬∗≠∅\mathcal{Q}^{\ast}\neq\varnothing and, for every q∈𝒬∗q\in\mathcal{Q}^{\ast},

Q0.025[Δ^q∗]>0,ECEq(θ′)≤0.10,accq​(θ′)>max⁡{accq​(rule),accq​(random),accq​(majority)},\begin{gathered}Q_{0.025}\bigl[\widehat{\Delta}_{q}^{\ast}\bigr]>0,\qquad\mathrm{ECE}_{q}(\theta^{\prime})\leq 0.10,\\ \mathrm{acc}_{q}(\theta^{\prime})>\max\bigl\{\mathrm{acc}_{q}(\mathrm{rule}),\,\mathrm{acc}_{q}(\mathrm{random}),\,\mathrm{acc}_{q}(\mathrm{majority})\bigr\},\end{gathered} (3)

where Δ^q=accq​(θ′)−accq​(θ)\widehat{\Delta}_{q}=\mathrm{acc}_{q}(\theta^{\prime})-\mathrm{acc}_{q}(\theta) is computed on identical states and Q0.025Q_{0.025} is the lower 2.5% quantile of its cluster-bootstrap replicates Δ^q∗\widehat{\Delta}_{q}^{\ast} over entities. ECE is the expected calibration error of the uncalibrated candidate, and “random” is the random-subset control. The full rule (equation (14)) adds a minimum of 200 labelled rows per question, a regression limit of one point and a refusal of candidates whose answers collapse onto one option. Release gates have been proposed for self-improving agent runtimes as an engineering safeguard64, and here the gate is also part of the scientific claim. The gate releases a version only if it beats its parent, the rule-based controller, the majority class and a random-subset control trained on the same number of rows, and every trained version, its data, checkpoint and verdict are kept in an append-only registry. When a round learns from execution-labelled benchmark states, each benchmark task is answered only by a version whose lineage never trained on its group, an out-of-fold scheme analogous to cross-fitting65 and stacked generalization66.

The first round shows why the gate needs a majority-class baseline. Decision labels are imbalanced: on the gate split, 92% of analysis-family labels belong to a single class and 87% of skill-relevance labels are negative (Extended Data Table 1). Version 0, the public checkpoint used zero-shot, scored 0.26 on analysis family against 0.92 for the majority class and 0.79 for the rule-based controller, and 0.02 on skill choice against 0.69 and 0.68 (Fig. 4b). The skill-choice score is also below the chance level of about 1/16 for 16 options. On answer type and answer format the checkpoint scored 0.40 and 0.44, against majority-class rates of 0.49 and 0.50, and only on error class, with ten classes, did it exceed the majority class (0.43 against 0.08; rule-based controller 0.85). The rule-based controller is itself below the majority class on four of the six questions, so it cannot expose a candidate that learned only the label prior. Under such imbalance accuracy misleads, the accuracy paradox67: a candidate that always gave the most frequent training label would score 0.92 on analysis family and 0.87 on skill relevance, tens of points above version 0, and of the baselines in equation (3) only the majority class is certain to refuse it. Balanced accuracy68 corrects for the imbalance, but the gate’s verdict rests on accuracy against the three baselines.

A judgement enters retraining as soon as it can be labelled without a model. Round 1 therefore trains the judgements that construction, verifiers or execution label on the curriculum: analysis family, answer type, skill choice and relevance, answer format and error class.

Training raised accuracy on every decision question, and the gains carried over to the agent’s own states

The first trained version, rsi-v2, was trained on 2,500 rows of curriculum decisions and raised accuracy over version 0 on all six questions of the gate split, with lower bounds above zero. Under the gate’s scoring, in which a skill choice is correct if it is among the state’s valid skills, analysis family rose from 0.26 to 0.99, skill choice from 0.04 to 0.86, skill relevance from 0.13 to 0.98, error class from 0.43 to 0.91, answer type from 0.40 to 0.93 and answer format from 0.44 to 0.85 (Fig. 4c). Its calibration error was at most 0.08 on every question.

Further rounds raised accuracy in the same way (Table 3). rsi-v5, trained on synthetic protocol decisions, raised accuracy over version 0 on all four questions of its gate split, with lower bounds above zero: analysis family from 0.11 to 0.53, answer type from 0.24 to 1.00, skill choice from 0.04 to 0.46 and skill relevance from 0.53 to 0.68. rsi-v6 was trained on a curriculum shaped by the agent’s own trajectories: its training mix, the number of rows per decision type, was set by the decision errors that the controllers made on the development halves of seqqa2 and protocolqa2 in the main run. Its rows came from the curriculum generators and the verified synthetic protocols with labels by construction, so no development item became a training row, and each arm was trained on 1,200 rows, 1,000 drawn for it and 200 shared replay rows (Methods). On a held-out gate split of 250 generated decisions per question, it raised accuracy over version 0 on all four questions, with lower bounds above zero: analysis family by 0.868 [0.819, 0.912], answer type by 0.656 [0.605, 0.707], skill choice by 0.844 [0.799, 0.885] and skill relevance by 0.452 [0.365, 0.532]. Because decision labels are imbalanced, we also report balanced accuracy, the mean recall over classes: every trained version exceeded the majority class on every question (24 of 24 question–split pairs, +0.12 to +0.81).

These gains carry over from generated decisions to the agent’s own states. Because only the decision model changes, a trained version can be scored on the agent’s own decision states from the held-out halves, whose items training never drew on (Methods). On these states, rsi-v6 raised analysis-family accuracy on seqqa2 from 0.056 to 1.000 (+0.944 [+0.908, +0.974]; calibration error from 0.449 to 0.015; one label value) and execution-labelled error-class accuracy from 0.174 to 0.408 (item-level paired difference +0.186 [+0.045, +0.329]), the two judgements on which version 0 was weakest on benchmark states (Extended Data Table 6). Training also made the decision model robust to option order: re-asked with the options in another order, the public checkpoint changed 37% [34%, 40%] of its answers, in line with the sensitivity reported for open-weight decision models16, and rsi-v6 changed 6% [4%, 8%] (750 choice questions on gate states). On the same states, the version trained on rows selected by the parent’s errors changed about half as many answers as a version trained on a random subset of the same size (5.6% [4.2%, 7.5%] against 11.3% [9.3%, 13.8%]), so error selection made the judgements more stable. The quantity that training targets and the gate certifies is decision accuracy. Whether a correct decision changes a task’s score depends further on whether the agent acts on it and on the headroom of the judgement (Fig. 2; Fig. 3c), which the main run measures with version 0 as its LAYA arm.

The seqqa2 baseline gain comes from a convention skill layer, measured apart from the decision layer

Skills and the decision layer can both shape a judgement, such as which convention to report, so we measured their contributions separately. SeqQA, seqqa2, BixBench-Verified-50 and protocolqa2 ran with skill release r04b. The other benchmarks ran with release r03. r04b adds a general sequence-computation layer and a separately named convention layer for LAB-Bench to r03, together with a patch to the protocol-audit skill. The conventions in that layer were taken from the published LAB-Bench 2 scoring code. Skills were developed only on the development half of seqqa2, split by a hash of the item identifier, and the held-out half was tested once per release. On those 196 held-out items, at high reasoning effort, accuracy was 90.8% with the convention layer and 77.4% without it (151 of 195 gradable items). The held-out comparison for r03 comes from a medium-effort run (76.0%, 149 of 196). In a paired ablation under the same conditions, high and medium effort differed within noise (Methods). On a random set of 60 SeqQA items, accuracy was 60 of 60 with the convention layer and 58 of 60 without it. On BixBench-Verified-50, r04b and r03 both answered 43 of 50 items correctly. The gain on seqqa2 therefore comes from the convention layer, and the seqqa2 baseline of the main run is reported with that provenance.

Between the earlier round and the main run, the JEV effect on seqqa2 changed from +0.008 to −0.041, a change of −0.048 [−0.081, −0.016], most of it in the synonymous-mutation family, and on SeqQA from +0.020 to +0.001 (Extended Data Fig. 5). On protocolqa2, which ran under both releases, r04b changed the baseline score by +0.030 [−0.013, +0.072] relative to r03, and the JEV effect changed from −0.018 under r03 to +0.031 under r04b, a change of +0.048 [−0.031, +0.127]. The r04b baseline took 91% longer per task, and the two series also differ in run time and in the frozen code tree, so this comparison does not isolate the skill effect. Between the earlier round and the main run, both the reasoning effort and the skill release changed. That comparison is reported as their joint effect.

A domain profile extends the same harness to laboratory-protocol troubleshooting

Laboratory-protocol troubleshooting needs different judgements from computational analysis. In protocolqa2 the agent reads a protocol and a reported failure, and it must name the step that caused the failure and the change that fixes it. The judgements are of a different kind. On the development half (62 items, about 17 graded runs each across the baseline rounds and controller arms), 780 of 1,060 graded answers were correct, and 14 items held 191 of the 280 wrong answers. Most wrong answers blamed a salient but standard parameter or step, located the fault at the wrong step, or used the protocol’s controls only in part; others were distracted by a second oddity, restored the wrong original value, missed an absent or swapped reagent or trusted an altered reference value in the document. These are diagnosis errors rather than routing errors. The default harness was built for computational analyses: its analysis families and answer types do not describe a protocol fix, and its skill shortlist ranked a general protocol-repository skill ahead of the matching wet-lab skills.

We therefore built a protocol profile of the harness. It applies only to tasks whose workspace contains a protocol document, and on other tasks the harness is unchanged. The profile ships with the skill release as a catalog of ten wet-lab domains and their skills, and it adds the answer type “protocol fix”. For the answer it asks three closed questions: whether the answer names one step, reagent or parameter with a concrete change, whether the cited step matches the protocol text the agent extracted, and whether the change would explain and fix the reported symptom. A failed attempt to read the protocol document triggers a fixed reminder that lists the text-extraction tools available in the sandbox. As with every message, no catalog entry, template or reminder contains an answer or item-specific content.

The profile was designed after the protocolqa2 results of the main run were seen, and it was tuned on a development half of protocolqa2. It is therefore exploratory and outside the hypotheses. On the 62 held-out items, tested once and held out from tuning, although their main-run outcomes under r03 had been seen, JEV with the protocol profile answered 0.823 correctly, against 0.758 for the baseline under the same development skill release (5 items gained, 1 lost, sign test P = 0.22). In the main run, three rounds of JEV and of the general-LLM controller with the protocol profile changed the score by +0.011 [−0.023, +0.045] and +0.035 [−0.002, +0.073] relative to the baseline, at 11.7% and 15.0% less wall-clock time, and by −0.021 and +0.035 relative to the same controllers under the default harness. With the local decision model as judge, the protocol profile raised the score by +0.060 [+0.014, +0.108] relative to the baseline at 7.9% fewer steps, and by +0.068 [+0.012, +0.128] relative to the same model under the default harness (two rounds; Extended Data Table 5).

On synthetic protocol probes, LAYA version 0 chose wet-lab domains correctly, but its answers to the three answer questions ran in the wrong direction. It rated a generic answer as more specific than a specific one, so the profile has LAYA abstain on those questions. To train them we built laya-proto from synthetic protocol data with labels by construction. Claude Opus 5.5 wrote 128 of the 154 protocols from domain and topic prompts written by the authors, without benchmark text. DeepSeek-V4-Pro, at maximum reasoning effort, wrote the remaining 26 from the same prompts. Each protocol came with four to six single-substring faults, each with an observation and its correction. Two verifiers checked every fault: a structural check, and an independent diff check that the faulted protocol differs from the clean one at exactly one line, at the stated step. Labels are assigned by construction from the teacher-written fault and its correction, which the diff verifier checks, and no model assigns a label. The domain and skill come from the generating topic, and the answer type from the scenario template. The three answer questions are labelled from candidate answers built to be correct, to cite a wrong step, to misquote the right step, or to stay generic. Splits are by topic group, so no protocol or topic crosses splits. A bench firewall, whose corpus was never sent to the teacher, rejected any protocol that shared a title or a word 8-gram with the protocolqa2 questions or reference answers (0 of 154), and any row whose state shared a word 8-gram with those texts or with the staged protocol files (535 training, 167 calibration and 247 gate rows). The gate judges domain, answer type, skill choice and skill relevance, and the three answer questions are kept with their held-out protocols. laya-proto was judged by the gate as rsi-v5 (above).

Probe design poses the same closed decisions over measured state

Probe design separates measuring from judging in the same way as analysis. A germline target enrichment panel uses hybridization probes to enrich selected genomic regions before sequencing. Its probes are useful only if they bind their targets and nothing else, remain thermodynamically stable without folding on themselves69, and cover each target evenly enough to be read70, 71, 72. Germline panels test all of these conditions, because paralogous gene families contain near-identical exons73, exons can be GC-extreme or shorter than a probe, and population alleles introduce mismatches at binding sites. In Operon-S1, probe design is divided along the same lines (Fig. 5a). Tools measure every sequence property: tiling with MrBait74, genome-wide alignment with BWA-MEM75 and BLAST76, nearest-neighbour melting temperature, hairpin and self-dimer checks, and coverage. A slow agent plans and handles exceptions over a shared panel state, in a pre-synthesis design loop and a post-experiment redesign loop. What remains are closed choices over the measured state among eight design actions: keep, densify, relax the GC or melting-temperature window, lengthen, shorten, tighten the specificity screen, escalate to another assay, or stop. The decision layer poses these choices as closed questions over the measured state.

The first of these decisions, per-probe quality control, was measured directly. On 150 held-out keep-or-redesign decisions (75 of each label; 25 target groups held out from training; labels from the genome-wide specificity screen), the hosted decision model answered 0.913 [0.857, 0.949] correctly, against 0.500 for the public LAYA checkpoint, the chance level of this balanced set (Methods). One rule over visible features, fitted to the labels, reproduces all 3,859 keep-or-redesign labels in-sample, so this decision serves to check the layer against a known answer. The decisions that remain open are the method and parameters for a region, the attribution of low coverage of unknown cause, the protocol for GC-extreme regions and the choice among candidate panels.

On a 123-target, 31,855-bp germline panel on GRCh3777, a default design of 549 probes (90 nt, 45-bp step) reached a mean per-target coverage of 88.4% (Fig. 5b). After genome-wide specificity screening, 207 probes passed, 24 targets kept at least one passing probe and 16 were fully covered, and mean per-target coverage by passing probes fell to 15.8% (Methods). Because 82 of the 123 targets belong to the C4A/C4B pair, the other 41 targets are also reported separately: their mean coverage fell from 71.2% to 47.5%, and all 16 fully covered targets are among them. A denser design (70 nt, 35-bp step) covered every target base before screening, yet only 21 of 123 targets were fully covered after it (mean 20.4%; 61.2% outside C4A/C4B), and a targeted rescreen of the gaps raised fully covered targets from 16 to 19. Design coverage, post-screen coverage and capture are therefore different quantities, and the design summary alone overstates what a panel covers after screening.

The remaining gaps had three causes, each calling for a different action (Fig. 5c): sequence shared with another locus, exons shorter than a probe and GC-rich intervals. In the complement C4A/C4B pair, 35 of 41 exon pairs are identical in sequence. Shared probes gave a mean per-target design coverage of 96.9% over the pair’s targets, and none passed screening, because no probe can tell the two genes apart. At four boundary targets in two high-identity paralog pairs, none of 1,342 candidate units yielded a gene-specific passing probe, whereas 571 of 839 passed at a more divergent target of one of these pairs. At eight further zero-coverage targets the best off-target similarity was 0.967–1.0, and an expanded screen of 1,049 candidates of 60–120 nt across 17 targets added 58 passing probes and no newly covered target. At such loci the appropriate action is to escalate to another assay. A 72-bp TP53 exon, by contrast, was not covered by any passing probe of the 90-nt design. The 70-nt, 35-bp-step design, which also widens the GC and thermodynamic windows, fully covered 10 of 11 TP53 targets, against 9 of 11 in the default design. A GC-rich interval in another target gene (71.9% GC; 46 of 71 120-bp windows above 70%) is the candidate for densification. When the same interval was densified in the 69-gene panel described below, 2 of 23 added 120-nt probes passed every thermodynamic threshold, and in a single spike-in experiment with one control and one supplemented library from reference DNA (NA12878)78, unnormalized mean depth over that interval was 2,586× and 3,090×, a single paired observation.

Laboratory capture shows what such a panel achieves. A 69-gene germline panel of 120-nt probes, designed by the probe-design agent, captured 73 human DNA samples in seven batches, with an on-target fraction of 78.3 ± 5.5% (mean ± s.d.), a median of 99.46% of target bases at ≥30× and 86 of 87 genotype-derived calls concordant with an orthogonal assay in 29 samples (three calls each; 98.9%; exact 95% CI 93.8–99.97% treating calls as independent) (Fig. 5d). Median on-target fraction ranged from 0.67 to 0.85 across batches, and uniformity also differed between batches. Compared with an initial design written in a single pass by a language-model agent without the structured pipeline, the agent’s design of that panel changed exon footprint coverage by more than 10 percentage points in 34 of 69 genes, raising 15 and lowering 19 (Fig. 5e). Its largest gain, C4A/C4B from 4.0% to 97.2%, came from shared probes that capture both paralogs and cannot tell them apart, the same limit that the current design meets. The 69-gene design overlapped 111 of the 123 targets of the current design (95 fully, 16 partially).

Discussion

In long-horizon biomedical agents the limit has moved from computation to judgement: most of the original agent’s lost items and surplus time came from judgements about conventions, skills, evidence and answer format rather than from the computation. Operon-S1 separates judging from doing and makes these judgements a layer of their own. Each judgement can be checked against a label, the decision model can be exchanged on fixed states, every judgement is traced to its consequence, and the local model answered in under a second at no request cost. With the local model as judge, the layer’s efficiency effects were specific to benchmarks, lower cost on SeqQA and fewer steps on protocolqa2, and the rule-based controller also reduced steps on SciAgentArena and seqqa2, which suggests that part of the value lies in posing the right question at the right point. Training on verifiable labels raised the accuracy of every trained version on every decision question, and the gains carried over to the agent’s own decision states on held-out items.

The fast decision model here takes the monitoring and control roles that Nelson and Narens13 describe. It monitors the state of slower deliberation and controls its course at every recurring judgement, from scoping the task to checking the answer, a role distinct from routing between cheap and expensive models17, 32. Monitoring is measured by how well each judgement matches its label. Control is measured by the interventional contrast of each arm against the no-op control (equation (1)). In the original agent’s trajectories, headroom differed between judgements (Fig. 2), and the judgements with the most headroom are those that execution can label, which suits a fast, calibrated model that abstains when unsure and learns from execution-derived labels. Protocol troubleshooting has its own map of judgements, and it enters through its own profile of the same harness. Probe design shows the same pattern: per-probe calls reduce to a rule, whereas choices of route, parameters and escalation remain closed decisions over measured state.

The design separates three quantities: whether a decision is right, whether the agent acts on it and whether the task is scored correct. Earlier work found the first and the last to diverge36. The no-op controller anchors the comparison, the provenance record links each decision to its outcome, and the promotion gate admits a new version only on evidence that the training loop does not itself generate (equations (3) and (14)). A scientific agent that distils its trajectories into skills79 gains reusable procedures, and the controller adds a measured decision layer.

The operon describes this division of labour: its regulator reads a signal and switches genes without making their products, and a different regulator can be swapped in without changing the genes. The decision layer reads the state of the run, acts only through fixed messages and can be exchanged without changing the agent. The layer is defined by its questions, actions and labels. Six controllers, from rules to a general language model, ran in the same harness on the same states, so the decision model can be exchanged without changing the agent, and a domain enters through a profile of the harness rather than a new architecture. It is likely to help when three conditions hold: (1) a task runs for tens of steps, so that judgements about conventions, routes, evidence and stopping recur; (2) those judgements can be posed as closed questions over a summary of the state; and (3) their correctness can be verified by execution or construction, so that the controller learns without model-generated labels. Computational analysis, laboratory-protocol troubleshooting and probe design all meet these conditions. On short single-step questions the controller’s fixed start-up cost dominates, and where a rule reproduces every decision, the rule suffices.

The evaluation covers one slow-system family, its computational work and protocol troubleshooting. The general-LLM arm poses the same closed questions to the model that drives the slow system, which bounds how much of the effect depends on a separate fast model. The protocol profile was tuned on the development half of protocolqa2 and tested once on the held-out half. Skill releases differ between benchmarks, so effects are compared within a benchmark (Methods). In the panel application the current design is computational, and its laboratory reference is the capture of the 69-gene panel.

These properties matter more in the life sciences than in most computational fields. A biological conclusion turns on conventions that a task rarely states, such as the genome build, the coordinate system, the normalization, the threshold and the direction of an effect8, and on attributions such as which step of a protocol failed. A wrong computational judgement costs a rerun, whereas a wrong judgement about a protocol or a probe design costs reagents, instrument time and an experimental cycle. Laboratory practice already answers this with records that let another scientist check each decision, and the provenance record gives an agent’s judgements the same form.

Through ProtoPilot’s protocol-to-instrument layer1, the same closed decisions, such as whether to densify, shorten or escalate, can be posed during wet-laboratory execution, where their labels come from the experiment itself. As agents move from analysis to instruments, the judgements that decide cost and outcome become a larger share of the work, and a decision layer that judges without doing, and that can be measured, replaced and trained under a gate, is the part of the system that has to be trusted.
