Methods

Slow system

The slow system is the ProtoPilot agent runtime1 (frozen commits 7d92ccb, 7417042 and cb88472, each recorded with its batches) driven by DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (API model deepseek-flash, build 1017, system fingerprint bc19ba97…) with reasoning effort set to high and a 786,432-token context window, beyond which the runtime compacts history. Language-model judges ran at maximum reasoning effort. All arms share one system prompt. Within a benchmark, all arms share one skill release. Release r03 (87 skills, manifest SHA-256 b02db3b6…) is used for BiomniBench-DA, SciAgentArena and OmicsBench. Release r04b (92 skills, manifest SHA-256 589b01cd…) is used for SeqQA, seqqa2, BixBench-Verified-50 and protocolqa2. r04b contains r03 and adds three things. The first is a general sequence-computation layer: rules for using only the sequences a task provides, six-frame scans of genomic windows and numeric precision, plus skills for melting temperature, molecular weight, sequence composition and complexity, and coding-sequence primer design. The second is a separately named convention layer for LAB-Bench, whose conventions were taken from the published LAB-Bench 2 scoring code and reproduce it on 3,000 synthetic sequences. The third is a patch to the protocol-audit skill. The held-out comparison used r04 and its ablation r04-noB, which removes the convention layer and every reference to it. They differ from r04b and r04b-noB only by the protocol-audit patch. Skills were developed only on the development half of seqqa2 (204 items, by parity of a SHA-256 hash of the item identifier), and the held-out half (196 items) was tested once per release. In a paired ablation on 61 seqqa2 items (41 that an earlier configuration answered correctly and r03 at medium effort did not, and 20 controls), r03 answered 33 correctly at high effort and 31 at medium effort (5 items right only at high effort, 3 only at medium, sign test P = 0.73). With the skills of the earlier configuration, which quoted benchmark wording and were therefore not used, it answered 58 and 54. No effect of the effort setting on seqqa2 was detectable at this sample size (5 against 3 discordant items), whereas the skills of the earlier configuration raised the counts from 33 and 31 to 58 and 54. No release contains item identifiers, sequences, answers or paraphrased items. A leak scan against all 400 seqqa2 items found no sequence, identifier or 25-mer hits, and one 8-gram of generic task wording. Skills are loaded on demand, agents may install packages into a per-task prefix and shared environments are read-only. Per-task time limits are twice the official limit where a benchmark publishes one (SciAgentArena, BiomniBench-DA) and twice the adapter’s default otherwise (600 s for SeqQA and seqqa2, 1,200 s for protocolqa2), identical for all arms (Table 2), and timed-out tasks score zero. For seqqa2 the final 60 s of the limit are reserved to collect a last answer, and items answered in this window are labelled as finalized after timeout. A forced final step sends the same explicit final-answer instruction in every arm; it is part of the unmodified agent and therefore of the no-op arm, and its text is identical in every batch of the main table.

Motivating trajectories

The trajectories of Fig. 2 (BixBench-Verified-50, SciAgentArena, seqqa2 and BiomniBench-DA) were recorded with the original agent in earlier rounds, under earlier skill and environment versions, on items that overlap the formal evaluation, and were used only to motivate the design. The values of ω\omega are single-run, time-weighted descriptive values; for SciAgentArena and seqqa2 the post-answer time is divided by the wall-clock time of all tasks, which bounds ω\omega from below. The skill-routing counts come from an earlier, smaller skill release. Each wrong BixBench-Verified-50 answer was read in full and assigned to one class. In these trajectories one item, whose reference range has its bounds reversed, could not be graded, so 49 of the 50 items are gradable. In the formal evaluation that range is graded between its two end points in every arm (Benchmarks, deviation (x)).

Decision points and states

A decision point is a tuple

d=(trigd,ρd,{(qd,j,𝒪d,j,κd,j)}j∈Jd),d=\Bigl(\mathrm{trig}_{d},\ \rho_{d},\ \{(q_{d,j},\mathcal{O}_{d,j},\kappa_{d,j})\}_{j\in J_{d}}\Bigr), (4)

where trigd​(ht)∈{0,1}\mathrm{trig}_{d}(h_{t})\in\{0,1\} decides whether the point fires on the history ht=(a1,o1,…,at,ot)h_{t}=(a_{1},o_{1},\ldots,a_{t},o_{t}) of agent actions and tool observations, ρd\rho_{d} renders the history into a state s=ρd​(ht)s=\rho_{d}(h_{t}), and each sub-question qd,jq_{d,j} has a finite option set 𝒪d,j\mathcal{O}_{d,j} and a type κd,j∈{choice,score,yes/no}\kappa_{d,j}\in\{\text{choice},\text{score},\text{yes/no}\}, with 𝒪d,j={0,1}\mathcal{O}_{d,j}=\{0,1\} for yes/no questions and four ordered levels for the score question of the long-computation check. Table 1 lists every decision point. States are rendered by pure functions of the task prompt, workspace listing, environments, skill shortlist and message history; they contain at most 900 tokens (state and questions together at most 1,024), with a fixed task excerpt (the first 1,200 and last 600 characters). Skill candidates are the top 15 BM251 matches over skill descriptions plus a no-skill option. States of a running task contain the last tool call’s name, command summary, status, exit code and duration, the tails of standard error (2,000 characters) and standard output (1,000), the budget fraction, loaded skills, a count of repeated commands and the tail of accumulated code (8,000 characters). Runs of 20 or more nucleotide characters are replaced by length placeholders. Option order is shuffled2 with a seed derived from the item and decision point and recorded. Conventions come from a registry of slots grouped by analysis type; each slot has a question, options with their meanings, patterns that detect when the task already states the convention and patterns that detect the value the agent used. The registry may not contain an option that is supported only by a proven benchmark defect.

Control policy

A controller ϕ\phi returns, for each sub-question, a distribution pϕ(⋅∣s,qd,j)∈𝒫(𝒪d,j)p_{\phi}(\cdot\mid s,q_{d,j})\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{O}_{d,j}), the set of distributions over 𝒪d,j\mathcal{O}_{d,j}; the rule-based and self-verification controllers return point masses and the no-op controller returns nothing. All controllers share the policy, thresholds and messages below and differ only in pϕp_{\phi}, except that the rule-based controller cannot end a run through P7 (see below). A fixed policy maps the distributions and two deterministic state facts, files⁡(s)\mathrm{files}(s) and best⁡(s)\mathrm{best}(s) (defined below), to an action and a message,

αd=πd({pϕ(⋅∣s,qd,j)}j∈Jd,s)∈{𝖻𝗋𝗂𝖾𝖿,𝗋𝖾𝗆𝗂𝗇𝖽,𝖿𝗈𝗋𝖼𝖾-𝖿𝗂𝗇𝖺𝗅,𝗋𝖾𝖼𝗁𝖾𝖼𝗄,𝖺𝖻𝗌𝗍𝖺𝗂𝗇},m=μ⁡(αd,y^)∈ℳ∪{∅},\begin{gathered}\alpha_{d}=\pi_{d}\bigl(\{p_{\phi}(\cdot\mid s,q_{d,j})\}_{j\in J_{d}},\,s\bigr)\in\{\mathsf{brief},\mathsf{remind},\mathsf{force\text{-}final},\mathsf{recheck},\mathsf{abstain}\},\\ m=\mu(\alpha_{d},\hat{y})\in\mathcal{M}\cup\{\varnothing\},\end{gathered} (5)

where y^j=arg⁡maxy​pϕ​(y∣s,qd,j)\hat{y}_{j}=\arg\max_{y}p_{\phi}(y\mid s,q_{d,j}), ℳ\mathcal{M} is a finite set of templates written in advance and ∅\varnothing denotes no message. Abstention sends no message. Templates may insert the names of files, environments or conventions, never an answer value. The action 𝖿𝗈𝗋𝖼𝖾​-​𝖿𝗂𝗇𝖺𝗅\mathsf{force\text{-}final} closes the tool loop and sends the final-answer instruction. A choice question yields an action only if its top option is both probable and separated from the runner-up,

p(1)≥τactandp(1)−p(2)≥δ,p_{(1)}\geq\tau_{\text{act}}\quad\text{and}\quad p_{(1)}-p_{(2)}\geq\delta, (6)

with τact=0.6\tau_{\text{act}}=0.6 and δ=0.2\delta=0.2. Two decision points can end the tool loop. The evidence check asks whether the evidence answers every part of the task (pdonep_{\text{done}}) and whether a required step is missing (pmissp_{\text{miss}}); the long-computation check rates four options and uses the probability of stopping with the best result so far (pstopp_{\text{stop}}):

πF1={𝖿𝗈𝗋𝖼𝖾​-​𝖿𝗂𝗇𝖺𝗅,pdone≥τdone∧pmiss≤τmiss∧¬files⁡(s),𝗋𝖾𝗆𝗂𝗇𝖽,pdone≥τdone∧pmiss≤τmiss∧files⁡(s),𝖺𝖻𝗌𝗍𝖺𝗂𝗇,otherwise,πP7={𝖿𝗈𝗋𝖼𝖾​-​𝖿𝗂𝗇𝖺𝗅,pstop≥τforce∧best⁡(s)∧ϕ≠rule∧¬files⁡(s),𝗋𝖾𝗆𝗂𝗇𝖽,pstop≥τstop​and the first case does not apply,𝖺𝖻𝗌𝗍𝖺𝗂𝗇,otherwise,\begin{gathered}\pi_{\mathrm{F1}}=\begin{cases}\mathsf{force\text{-}final},&p_{\text{done}}\geq\tau_{\text{done}}\wedge p_{\text{miss}}\leq\tau_{\text{miss}}\wedge\neg\,\mathrm{files}(s),\\ \mathsf{remind},&p_{\text{done}}\geq\tau_{\text{done}}\wedge p_{\text{miss}}\leq\tau_{\text{miss}}\wedge\mathrm{files}(s),\\ \mathsf{abstain},&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\\[4.0pt] \pi_{\mathrm{P7}}=\begin{cases}\mathsf{force\text{-}final},&p_{\text{stop}}\geq\tau_{\text{force}}\wedge\mathrm{best}(s)\wedge\phi\neq\mathrm{rule}\wedge\neg\,\mathrm{files}(s),\\ \mathsf{remind},&p_{\text{stop}}\geq\tau_{\text{stop}}\ \text{and the first case does not apply},\\ \mathsf{abstain},&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\end{gathered} (7)

where files⁡(s)\mathrm{files}(s) marks tasks answered through output files (BiomniBench-DA and SciAgentArena), for which ending the tool loop would prevent any answer from being written, and best⁡(s)\mathrm{best}(s) that the state records a best result so far. The rule-based controller never ends a run through P7, because its stopping signal is a budget fraction rather than a judgement of progress, and it reminds instead. Thresholds were fixed in the decision-layer configuration before any formal benchmark run and are shared by all controllers: τformat=0.3\tau_{\text{format}}=0.3 (the answer check requests a recheck when the probability that the answer meets its stated format falls below it), τact=0.6\tau_{\text{act}}=0.6, δ=0.2\delta=0.2, τdone=0.85\tau_{\text{done}}=0.85, τmiss=0.15\tau_{\text{miss}}=0.15, τstop=0.8\tau_{\text{stop}}=0.8, τforce=0.9\tau_{\text{force}}=0.9. The evidence check is asked at most once per task, there is at most one recheck, which requires at least 60 s of remaining budget and is not used for file-answered tasks, and the controller makes at most 60 requests per task, answering every trigger that fires at the same time in a single request. OmicsBench is a multi-turn session benchmark on which the decision layer is inert; it is run in the baseline arm only, and the controller arms run on the other six benchmarks.

No-op equivalence and attribution

Let reqϕ​(ht)\mathrm{req}^{\phi}(h_{t}) be the model request that the agent issues after history hth_{t} under controller ϕ\phi, and req⁡(ht)\mathrm{req}(h_{t}) that of the unmodified agent. On every history in its test suite, a regression test enforces

reqϕ0​(ht)=req⁡(ht),\mathrm{req}^{\phi_{0}}(h_{t})=\mathrm{req}(h_{t}), (8)

so that, apart from latency, the agent under the no-op controller behaves as the original agent, and equation (1) contrasts interventions that differ only in the controller. Budget fractions in the state are computed from wall-clock time in every arm. The provenance record supports a diagnostic decomposition of Δϕ\Delta_{\phi} over decision points,

Δϕ=∑dPr[trigd]Pr[αd≠𝖺𝖻𝗌𝗍𝖺𝗂𝗇∣trigd]Pr[Ad=1∣αd≠𝖺𝖻𝗌𝗍𝖺𝗂𝗇,trigd]γd+ξ,γd=𝔼[Y(ϕ)−Y(ϕ0)∣Ad=1,trigd],\begin{gathered}\Delta_{\phi}=\sum_{d}\Pr[\mathrm{trig}_{d}]\;\Pr[\alpha_{d}\neq\mathsf{abstain}\mid\mathrm{trig}_{d}]\;\Pr[A_{d}=1\mid\alpha_{d}\neq\mathsf{abstain},\mathrm{trig}_{d}]\;\gamma_{d}\;+\;\xi,\\ \gamma_{d}=\mathbb{E}\bigl[Y(\phi)-Y(\phi_{0})\mid A_{d}=1,\mathrm{trig}_{d}\bigr],\end{gathered} (9)

where AdA_{d} indicates that the agent adopted the action. The remainder ξ\xi is zero if non-adopted actions have no effect, each decision point fires at most once and the effects of adopted actions at different points add. Because AdA_{d} and trigd\mathrm{trig}_{d} are defined under ϕ\phi, γd\gamma_{d} is not identified from the data, and the adopted-versus-non-adopted contrast we report is descriptive.

Post-answer fraction

For equation (2), time is measured from the start of the task, ti∗t_{i}^{\ast} is the timestamp of the first tool observation whose output contains the submitted value after normalization of number formatting (numbers rounded to the submitted precision, sequences matched as substrings, trivial values not located), and II is the set of tasks for which such an observation exists; for SciAgentArena, ti∗t_{i}^{\ast} is the end of the first run of the solution script that exits successfully. ω\omega is a ratio of summed times.

Monitoring resolution

The evidence check is posed before the agent’s next model request, and the agent’s answer almost always arrives in its last message, so in the main run the check fired twice and no evidence-check state had a located answer time. The resolution measure below could therefore not be estimated. Monitoring is evaluated on the states recorded under the no-op controller, which never intervenes, by replaying them through each controller offline. Let 𝒮+\mathcal{S}^{+} and 𝒮−\mathcal{S}^{-} be evidence-check states in tasks that were scored correct, at times t≥ti∗t\geq t_{i}^{\ast} and t<ti∗t<t_{i}^{\ast} respectively. Both sets come from solved tasks and are separated by whether the answer is already in hand; because the evidence check fires at most once per task, the comparison is between tasks. The monitoring resolution of controller ϕ\phi, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve3 as used for metacognitive sensitivity4, is the probability that it rates a state in which the answer is already in hand above one in which it is not,

AUROCϕ=Pr[pdoneϕ(s+)>pdoneϕ(s−)]+12Pr[pdoneϕ(s+)=pdoneϕ(s−)],\mathrm{AUROC}_{\phi}=\Pr\bigl[p_{\text{done}}^{\phi}(s^{+})>p_{\text{done}}^{\phi}(s^{-})\bigr]+\tfrac{1}{2}\Pr\bigl[p_{\text{done}}^{\phi}(s^{+})=p_{\text{done}}^{\phi}(s^{-})\bigr], (10)

with s+∈𝒮+s^{+}\in\mathcal{S}^{+} and s−∈𝒮−s^{-}\in\mathcal{S}^{-} drawn independently; it is defined when both sets are non-empty. It is 0.5 for a controller that carries no information about the agent’s progress. Its calibration on the same states is reported as ECE. Replay uses the deployed per-request timeouts. Intervals are cluster-bootstrap intervals over tasks.

Controllers and serving

All controllers share one client, which sends the state and questions, does not follow redirects, applies per-request time budgets, retries once on rate-limit or server errors and validates the response schema. JEV, LAYA and the general-LLM controller have the same budgets: 30 s for each request, 45 s for each request of the brief, and 92 s for the brief in total. The general-LLM controller sends the same states and questions to DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at high reasoning effort. A timed-out or failed request leads to abstention and never fails a task. Keys exist only in the orchestrator process and never in the sandbox. The hosted controller calls JEV14 (served version jev-1.14.0 on every request). The time budgets of JEV and LAYA were raised to equal those of the general-LLM controller after the main run had started (Deviations during the main run). The local controller calls a server bound to loopback on dedicated CPU cores (four replicas of eight cores behind a local proxy), which agents cannot reach because the egress proxy refuses loopback and private addresses. LAYA version 0 is the public multilingual checkpoint47 (revision e4e9ddf); trained versions are registered by name and served by the same process.

Synthetic curriculum

The curriculum has 25 task families covering sequence, alignment, primer, cloning, statistics and omics computations. After removal of four training tasks flagged by a contamination check, it contains 1,517 tasks (1,373 parent tasks and 144 perturbation siblings). Sequences come from public European Nucleotide Archive5 references, and sequences that occur inside benchmark items are blacklisted. Each task has two independent implementations and metamorphic checks; before the removal, the verifier accepted every reference answer and rejected all 7,681 constructed negatives, and two independent recomputations, of 100 and of 200 tasks, found no errors (exact two-sided 95% upper bounds6 3.6% and 1.8%; 1.5% one-sided for the 200 tasks). Splits are grouped by entity, with no entity in more than one split: 972 training, 201 development, 232 test and 112 out-of-distribution tasks. For retraining, about 10% of training entities, chosen by entity hash, form a calibration split and the rest the training pool; development and test together form the gate split (433 tasks); the out-of-distribution split is read by no selection step. Contamination checks against all benchmarks (8-gram overlap, canary strings, identifiers) found no further hits.

Decision synthesis

Four generators (G1–G3, G5) call the controller’s renderer and question functions. G1 labels analysis family and answer type from frozen maps. G2 labels skill relevance from a frozen family-to-skill map, with no-skill rows capped at 25%. G3 builds compliant and non-compliant final answers in a 1:1 ratio, and compliant answers must pass the task verifier. A fifth generator, G4, builds convention mismatches where a task’s constructed negatives map onto a registered slot; it is not used in round 1. G5 injects faults of ten classes into code run in a sandbox (unprivileged user, no network, 20-s timeout, address-space limit) and labels each case with the injected class, kept only when execution fails with that class; in round 1 it ran 10,000 template cases (1,000 per class), discarding cases that exited successfully or duplicated an existing state. Round-1 prose and fault code come from templates. In teacher variants, a language model writes prose around answer and convention placeholders that must be preserved verbatim and writes fault-inducing code; it never sees benchmark text and never produces a label, and its calls are cached by prompt hash and capped in cost. Round 1 produced 12,413 training, 2,561 calibration, 8,281 gate and 1,712 out-of-distribution rows before the firewall (Extended Data Table 1).

Leakage firewall

Every row rr with state ss carries a label-source tag λ⁡(r)\lambda(r), a source benchmark, a generator and a lineage that names the batches and arms it derives from. A row enters training only if

admit⁡(r)=\displaystyle\mathrm{admit}(r)={} 𝟙[schema(r)] 1[¬comp(r)] 1[lineage(r)declared] 1[λ(r)∈Λ]\displaystyle\mathds{1}[\mathrm{schema}(r)]\;\mathds{1}[\neg\,\mathrm{comp}(r)]\;\mathds{1}[\mathrm{lineage}(r)\ \text{declared}]\;\mathds{1}[\lambda(r)\in\Lambda] (11)
×𝟙[maxrun(s)<20] 1[h(s)∉H] 1[G8(exc(s))∩(G8(ℬ)∖G8bp)=∅]=1,\displaystyle\times\mathds{1}[\mathrm{maxrun}(s)<20]\;\mathds{1}[h(s)\notin H]\;\mathds{1}\bigl[G_{8}(\mathrm{exc}(s))\cap(G_{8}(\mathcal{B})\setminus G_{8}^{\mathrm{bp}})=\varnothing\bigr]=1,

where schema\mathrm{schema} requires every field to be present, comp\mathrm{comp} marks lineage through the hosted comparator directly or through any batch that ran a comparator arm, Λ={construction,verifier,execution}\Lambda=\{\text{construction},\text{verifier},\text{execution}\} (no human-labelled rows exist), maxrun\mathrm{maxrun} is the longest run of nucleotide characters, HH is the set of hashes of evaluation states, exc⁡(s)\mathrm{exc}(s) is the task excerpt of the state, G8​(ℬ)G_{8}(\mathcal{B}) is the set of word 8-grams in the task prompts of the six benchmarks evaluated when the round-1 data were built (protocolqa2, added later, is checked against the same rules) and G8bpG_{8}^{\mathrm{bp}} the boilerplate grams of the benchmark prompts that occur in at least max⁡(5,⌈0.02​N⌉)\max(5,\lceil 0.02N\rceil) of the NN prompts. In round 1, with no benchmark states in training, HH and ℬ\mathcal{B} cover all benchmark items. When benchmark states enter training under cross-fitting, HH and ℬ\mathcal{B} are restricted to the items of the held-out group. Duplicate state–question pairs are refused at selection. Counts of each rejection class are given in Extended Data Table 1.

Hard-example mining

Within each question, rows are sampled without replacement by taking the largest keys ui1/wiu_{i}^{1/w_{i}} with ui∼U⁡(0,1)u_{i}\sim\mathrm{U}(0,1)7, with weight

wi=(12+12min⁡(ℓi,5)5)(1+𝟙[y^i≠yi∧p(1),i≥τact]),w_{i}=\Bigl(\tfrac{1}{2}+\tfrac{1}{2}\,\tfrac{\min(\ell_{i},5)}{5}\Bigr)\bigl(1+\mathds{1}[\hat{y}_{i}\neq y_{i}\wedge p_{(1),i}\geq\tau_{\text{act}}]\bigr), (12)

where ℓi\ell_{i} is the parent version’s negative log-likelihood of the label (probabilities floored at 10−610^{-6}; ℓi=5\ell_{i}=5 if the parent gave no answer), y^i\hat{y}_{i} its top option and p(1),ip_{(1),i} that option’s probability (max⁡(p,1−p)\max(p,1-p) for yes/no questions). In round 1 the parent is version 0. A total budget of 2,500 rows is allocated across questions by largest remainder. The random-subset control uses the same per-question quotas, sampled uniformly from an independent stream seeded by SHA-256(“13|random”).

Training and calibration

Models were fine-tuned from the public checkpoint with the vendor training tool47 on CPU, using soft cross-entropy, shuffled options, maximum length 1,024 tokens (matching the served state budget), seed 13, an effective batch of 64 (micro-batch 1, gradient accumulation 64, 8 threads, identical for candidate and control) and 3 epochs, as an unprivileged user without network access and without swap. Candidate and control were trained under a 12-GiB memory cap with identical selections. Runs with fewer than 100 optimizer updates are refused and training logs are scanned for collapse warnings. A checkpoint’s identity is the SHA-256 of its sorted file hashes. Calibration uses temperature scaling58: each question qq receives a temperature

βq=argminβ∈𝒢1nq∑i∈𝒟cal,q−logsoftmax(logpi/β)yi,𝒢={0.25⋅16j/63}j=063,\beta_{q}=\arg\min_{\beta\in\mathcal{G}}\ \frac{1}{n_{q}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{cal},q}}-\log\,\mathrm{softmax}\bigl(\log p_{i}/\beta\bigr)_{y_{i}},\qquad\mathcal{G}=\{0.25\cdot 16^{j/63}\}_{j=0}^{63}, (13)

with βq=1\beta_{q}=1 if nq<30n_{q}<30 or if the improvement in negative log-likelihood is at most 10−610^{-6}; thresholds are not refitted. The frozen benchmark code serves raw checkpoint probabilities, so each candidate is gated both uncalibrated and calibrated, and only an uncalibrated pass can promote a version into the benchmark arm.

Promotion gate

The gate judges each question kind q∈𝒬q\in\mathcal{Q} (relevance questions for different skills are pooled; convention fit is excluded in round 1; rules gate-rules@2, SHA-256 70459d6f…), with headroom set 𝒬∗={q:accq​(rule)≤0.95}\mathcal{Q}^{\ast}=\{q:\mathrm{acc}_{q}(\mathrm{rule})\leq 0.95\}. With Δ^q\widehat{\Delta}_{q} as in equation (3), computed on identical state hashes,

promote⁡(θ′)⇔\displaystyle\mathrm{promote}(\theta^{\prime})\iff{} 𝒬∗≠∅\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}^{\ast}\neq\varnothing (14)
∧∀q∈𝒬:nq≥200∧Δ^q≥−0.01∧modeq(θ′)−modeq(y)≤0.20\displaystyle\wedge\;\forall q\in\mathcal{Q}:\ n_{q}\geq 200\ \wedge\ \widehat{\Delta}_{q}\geq-0.01\ \wedge\ \mathrm{mode}_{q}(\theta^{\prime})-\mathrm{mode}_{q}(y)\leq 0.20
∧∀q∈𝒬∗:conditions (3)\displaystyle\wedge\;\forall q\in\mathcal{Q}^{\ast}:\ \text{conditions (3)}
∧accq​(random)≥accq​(majority)−0.05,\displaystyle\wedge\ \mathrm{acc}_{q}(\mathrm{random})\geq\mathrm{acc}_{q}(\mathrm{majority})-0.05,

where a question that the rule-based controller does not answer counts as incorrect for it, and modeq\mathrm{mode}_{q} is the share of the most frequent answer and the majority control answers the modal training label. When the modal label share is at least 0.80 the collapse rule cannot bind, and such questions are protected only by the requirement to beat the majority class. Calibration error8 is

ECEq=∑k=110|Bk|nq​|acc⁡(Bk)−conf⁡(Bk)|\mathrm{ECE}_{q}=\sum_{k=1}^{10}\frac{|B_{k}|}{n_{q}}\,\bigl|\mathrm{acc}(B_{k})-\mathrm{conf}(B_{k})\bigr|

over ten equal-width bins of top-option probability; nqn_{q} counts the answered gate rows, empty bins contribute zero, and for yes/no questions only bins from 0.5 upwards can be occupied. Q0.025Q_{0.025} in equation (3) is the 2.5th percentile of a percentile cluster bootstrap9 (10,000 resamples, seed 13) over entities, or over fault templates for error classes. Verdicts other than promotion are distinguished: insufficient evidence (nq<200n_{q}<200), insufficient headroom (𝒬∗=∅\mathcal{Q}^{\ast}=\varnothing) and reject. A random-subset control more than 0.05 below the majority class is unhealthy, and the verdict is then insufficient evidence. Control accuracy is computed only on rows that ask the question. A constructed candidate that always answers the most frequent training label, with one-hot or calibrated probabilities, fails the gate in every configuration (20 of 20). An audit found that the first version of the gate could pass a candidate that learned only the label prior, before that version judged any candidate. The revised rules (gate-rules@2, SHA-256 70459d6f…) judged every candidate reported here. Training rows of three curriculum families whose prompts contained their own answers were removed before training. For rsi-v6, decision errors of the non-comparator controllers were mined from the graded records of the development halves only (held-out records were skipped before they were opened). The counts per decision type set how many rows each type received, and the rows themselves were new curriculum tasks from fresh generator seeds and re-rendered verified protocols, with labels by construction. The candidate and its random-subset control each drew 1,000 rows from the same pool and shared 200 replay rows (1,200 training rows per arm), the gate split was held out from that pool, and the leakage firewall was applied before either arm was drawn. Offline gate replays use the same 30-s timeout for every controller. Option-order sensitivity was measured by replaying 1,000 gate states with every choice question asked again under a different option order and counting changed answers, with Wilson 95% intervals. Only the public checkpoint may serve as a root of the registry.

Cross-fitting

For the promoted arm, each benchmark task xx is assigned to a group g⁡(x)=SHA​-​256​(key⁡(x))modKg(x)=\mathrm{SHA\text{-}256}(\mathrm{key}(x))\bmod K with K=5K=5; the key is the data capsule for BixBench-Verified-50, the data directory for SciAgentArena and the subtask and item for the others. The promoted arm answers xx with

ψ⁡(x)=the latest promoted version ​θ​ with ​g​(x)∉trainedOn⁡(θ),\psi(x)=\text{the latest promoted version }\theta\text{ with }g(x)\notin\mathrm{trainedOn}(\theta), (15)

where trainedOn⁡(θ)\mathrm{trainedOn}(\theta) is the union of the groups on which θ\theta and all its ancestors were trained; for version 0 it is empty, so ψ⁡(x)\psi(x) always exists. The arm is a mixture of versions. The routing manifest is frozen and hashed before the arm runs. In the main run every task is answered by version 0. Benchmark states entered training only through a parity split of seqqa2 and protocolqa2, the even and odd values of SHA-256 of the item identifier: errors were mined only from the development halves, and in-loop evaluations use only the held-out halves (196 and 62 items).

Protocol profile and protocol training data

The protocol profile is selected per arm and applies per task only when the workspace holds a protocol document (a staged text, PDF or word-processor file whose name or prompt refers to a protocol). Without it, every request and every injected message is byte-identical to the default harness, which a regression test checks. On protocol tasks the evidence, long-computation, error, convention and out-of-bounds checks do not fire. The brief asks at most six questions, among them the domain, the skill, the answer type and the relevance of up to two candidate skills. The answer check requests one recheck when the probability that the answer is specific, or that the change explains the symptom, falls below 0.25. Whether the cited step matches the extracted text is recorded only, because on development transcripts it did not separate correct from incorrect answers. The answer check reads the protocol lines only from the agent’s own tool output, and the harness never reads task files itself. The profile arms ran JEV and the general-LLM controller for three rounds each, and LAYA version 0 for two rounds, on protocolqa2 under r04b. For laya-proto, the teacher was Claude Opus 5.5, called through its command-line interface without tools or project context at medium reasoning effort. DeepSeek-V4-Pro, at maximum reasoning effort, wrote the 26 protocols for which Opus returned no structured output. It wrote protocols, faults and facts, and it never produced a label. Each of the eleven domain classes (the ten wet-lab domains and a general class) has seven topic groups with two variants each, 154 protocols in all, and a SHA-256 hash of the group assigns four groups to training, one to calibration and two to the gate. The answer questions of gate and calibration protocols are written to separate held-out files and never enter the gate or calibration rows. Every row carries the lineage of its teacher call and no lineage through the comparator.

Comparator

JEV is used only as an inference-time comparator. Under the provider’s terms its outputs are never used as labels, rewards, curricula or selection signals, which the builder, gate and registry enforce through lineage checks. Conclusions about the local controller and its retraining do not depend on it.

Benchmarks and deviations from official settings

SeqQA and seqqa2 report accuracy; BixBench-Verified-50 uses the official open-answer protocol (first answer block, with a language-model judge for range answers); SciAgentArena reports mean correctness, OmicsBench the mean node score and BiomniBench-DA the mean rubric score (0–100). Timeouts score zero. Network policy follows each benchmark: BiomniBench-DA and OmicsBench had web access through a logged proxy that refused benchmark-data hosts, SciAgentArena and protocolqa2 were offline, and SeqQA, seqqa2 and BixBench-Verified-50 used an allowlist of scientific databases that excluded answer sources. Deviations: (i) BiomniBench-DA used the 50 tasks of its public release and ran natively in our sandbox rather than in its container harness, with 2 CPUs and 16 GiB per task; all 50 task images only copy the data directory, which we confirmed. (ii) Its judge script and rubrics were unchanged, but the judge model was DeepSeek-V4-Pro instead of Gemini 3.5 Flash, with maximum output raised from 8,192 to 32,768 tokens because the judge’s reasoning otherwise truncated its JSON. (iii) BixBench-Verified-50 range answers were judged by DeepSeek-V4-Pro. (iv) OmicsBench’s private test set is unavailable, so its three public tasks were run. (v) SciAgentArena used its 189 publicly reproducible tasks. (vi) BixBench-Verified-50 sets no memory limit; we used 16 GiB and 2 CPUs per task. (vii) Every batch runs on a frozen commit recorded with it. The main table combines two frozen commits that differ only in the time budgets of JEV and LAYA, and rounds started under earlier configurations are excluded. (viii) Time limits are doubled as stated under Slow system. (ix) One R annotation package that would otherwise download gene sets at run time was given a sealed, read-only local cache, identical for all arms. (x) BixBench-Verified-50 item a4d8a810 gives its reference range as (−0.064, −0.084), and we grade it on (−0.084, −0.064). (xi) protocolqa2 publishes no per-task limit, so its limit is twice the adapter’s default of 1,200 s, and its open answers are graded with the official labbench2 evaluation prompt by DeepSeek-V4-Pro. Its protocol files are staged from a local copy checked against SHA-256 digests. (xii) When the BiomniBench-DA judge ended a response without any text, the identical request was sent again, at most three times in total and within the verifier time limit. Every request is counted in the judge cost and recorded per task.

Deviations during the main run

The main run started at 01:48 (UTC+8) on 29 October 2026. It departed from its plan in the following ways. Each departure is recorded with the batches it affects, and the analysis rules were fixed before the affected results were computed. All times are UTC+8.

(a) Disk full. Between 01:58 and 02:40 the data volume filled twice. Two BiomniBench-DA tasks staged a full 17.9-GB copy of one count matrix per attempt, and 22 such copies accumulated. The volume was enlarged, and the interrupted batches were resumed under the same identities, configurations and commit. Graded records that showed a disk-full error (313 records, plus 18 that showed it only in the transcript) were not used. Each was replaced by a rerun of the same task under the same configuration, unless its whole batch had already been superseded by a later rerun. No affected task was left without a clean graded record. In a sensitivity analysis, every task with an attempt that started in the 01:58–02:40 window is removed from all arms of its benchmark.

(b) Isolation audit of protocolqa2. The frozen list of answer hosts had no entry for protocolqa2, so its batches were audited with the protocolqa2 hosts added (Evaluation integrity).

(c) Time budgets of JEV and LAYA. At 03:32 the JEV and LAYA batches on BiomniBench-DA and SciAgentArena were stopped at about 20% completion. They were rerun on a second frozen commit in which JEV and LAYA have the same time budgets as the general-LLM controller, 30 s for each request and 45 s for each request of the brief, instead of the shorter budgets of the first commit. In the main table, JEV and LAYA come from this commit and the other arms from the first. The two commits differ only in these budgets. The stopped batches are kept as evidence for the shorter budgets and are not in the main table.

(d) Concurrency on BiomniBench-DA. After the resume in (a), BiomniBench-DA ran at a concurrency of 3 instead of 6. The baseline, no-op, rule-based, self-verification and general-LLM batches ran partly at 6 and partly at 3, and the JEV and LAYA batches at 3 throughout. Because concurrency changes wall-clock time, the wall-clock and step changes of JEV and LAYA on BiomniBench-DA are shown for reference and do not count towards H1. Their score changes count towards H1.

(e) Host oversubscription and the seqqa2 relaunch. At about 05:30 the host load reached 845 on 96 cores. In the seqqa2 batches running at that point, 185 items had been graded, 36% to 62% of them per batch had reached the time limit, and the median wall-clock time per batch was 750 to 1,029 s, against 75 s in the relaunched baseline round. All seqqa2 batches were stopped and relaunched at lower concurrency under new batch identities, with the same configuration, skill release and commit. Only the relaunched batches enter the analysis, and the stopped batches are kept as evidence of the overload. A second SeqQA baseline round stopped at 13 of 600 items when the service manager timed out creating task slices. Its replacement was paused at 137 of 600 items and enters only σb\sigma_{b}.

(f) Paused baseline rounds. From 05:40, baseline rounds 2–5 on SciAgentArena, BiomniBench-DA and protocolqa2 were paused so that the first round of every arm could finish, and they were resumed later under the same identities. A baseline round enters the reference only if it covers at least 90% of the items of the most complete round. Extended Data Table 2 reports the number of rounds RR that entered on each benchmark. Where R<5R<5, the between-round standard deviation and the margin use the actual RR, and where R=1R=1 the margin is undefined and non-inferiority is not judged.

(g) Skill releases. Benchmarks use different releases (Slow system). Effects are reported per benchmark and never pooled across releases. r04b was developed on the seqqa2 development half, so the seqqa2 baseline of the main run may be optimistic. The protocolqa2 main results come from a rerun under r04b that started at 04:06. The first protocolqa2 run, under r03, is reported only as a skill ablation, which also differs in run time and commit.

(h) Protocol profile. The protocol profile of the harness was designed after the first protocolqa2 results were seen and was tuned on a development half of protocolqa2. Its arms, JEV and the general-LLM controller for three rounds each and LAYA version 0 for two rounds, ran on a third frozen commit that adds only the profile. They are reported as exploratory, outside Extended Data Table 2 and outside H1 and H2.

(i) Baseline and no-op. Baseline rounds run the original agent without the harness, and the no-op arm runs in round 1 only. The empirical check of equation (8) is therefore the no-op round against the mean of the baseline rounds.

(j) Earlier round. An earlier round at medium reasoning effort is used only for the motivating analyses and the effort comparison. During that round, test suites run on the same host killed tool processes of about 140 live tasks in three windows. These tasks are excluded from every arm of the earlier round. The main run is a new run at high effort, on code in which tests stop only their own units. In the same earlier round, the long-computation check never fired because its timing function rejected the decoded time stamps. Its controller effects therefore come from the other decision points. The main run uses the corrected code.

Evaluation integrity

Each task ran in new network, mount and process namespaces with a private process table, on a minimal root assembled from read-only bind mounts (system directories, the benchmark’s environments, reference data and the task’s skill snapshot) plus one writable workspace, as an unprivileged user with no capabilities and no privilege escalation. Home, temporary and cache directories were per task, and tasks run offline had no network socket. File tools resolve real paths and refuse writes through symbolic links, and graders that execute agent code run as an unprivileged user in their own process namespace. Before each round, a pre-flight probe had to fail every attempt to read other tasks, earlier rounds, gold answers, grader environments or host files; after each batch, an audit checked for requests that reached an answer host, file-tool paths outside the workspace, the skill snapshot and the agent’s own toolchain, new writes to host directories and private sentinels in transcripts and workspaces, and any of these voided the batch. Over the 96 batches of the main table (71 cells and 25 reruns after the disk-full incident; 11,880 records), none met a voiding condition: no request reached an answer host (the proxy blocked 3), and no host write or sentinel hit occurred. Rounds, arms and controller versions carry separate batch identities and cannot be merged or resumed across configurations. Because BiomniBench-DA permits web access, each run was audited after the fact against a table of source studies covering 14 of its 50 tasks; scores are reported over all and over unflagged tasks, and flagged counts are lower bounds. We checked that each language-model judge separates answers of different quality by submitting a strong, a deliberately weakened and an empty answer on three tasks per benchmark. The BiomniBench-DA judge scored them 100/44/0, 100/59/0 and 93/53/0. The BixBench-Verified-50 judge scored 1/0/0 on all three tasks in one run; in another it rejected one strong answer, a verdict it gave once in five gradings of that answer, and we report this variance with its scores. The check exposed a bug in our BiomniBench-DA bridge, which returned an error where the official script scores empty output as zero; it was fixed before these results. Every grader was audited with reproducing scripts. The official seqqa2 validators contain defects, among them water subtracted twice in molecular weight, primer checks on one strand, substring matching of gene names and a unit error in KmK_{\mathrm{m}}, and the BiomniBench-DA rubric parser drops negative levels. Main tables report official scores unchanged. Every completed batch in the main table, including the resource-failure reruns, passed the isolation audit, with no network request to an answer source and no file access outside the workspace, the skill snapshot and the agent’s toolchain.

Statistics

Each arm is paired with the baseline on the same tasks, with the per-task mean of the baseline rounds as reference (R=5R=5 scheduled; Extended Data Table 2 gives the rounds that entered). 95% confidence intervals are cluster-bootstrap intervals over group keys (10,000 resamples, seed 13). Infrastructure failures are excluded and counted. Timeouts keep the official score, which is zero on BiomniBench-DA. Tasks missing from any baseline round or from the arm are excluded and counted. The non-inferiority margin10 for benchmark bb is

εb=2.8​σbR,\varepsilon_{b}=\frac{2.8\,\sigma_{b}}{\sqrt{R}}, (16)

where σb\sigma_{b} is the standard deviation of the per-round mean headline score of the baseline over the paired tasks, computed from every baseline round with at least 30 graded tasks, and RR is the number of reference rounds (Extended Data Table 2). A benchmark with R=1R=1 receives no non-inferiority verdict. The constant 2.8 (z0.975+z0.80z_{0.975}+z_{0.80}, for α=0.05\alpha=0.05 and power 0.8) is a power-calculation quantity, and we use it as a margin rather than as a detectable difference. For R=5R=5 the margin is 1.25​σb1.25\,\sigma_{b}. The margin does not include the run-to-run variation of a single-round arm. A wider margin, 2.8​σb​1+1/R2.8\,\sigma_{b}\sqrt{1+1/R}, which includes it, is reported alongside as a sensitivity analysis and is not used for any verdict. H1 holds if the paired relative change in wall-clock time or in steps has an upper bound below zero on at least four of the five hypothesis benchmarks, every hypothesis benchmark with a verdict is non-inferior (lower bound above −εb-\varepsilon_{b}) and controller costs are included. H2 holds if, on SeqQA and seqqa2, JEV beats the self-verification control with a lower bound above zero in score or an upper bound below zero in efficiency. Because H1 and H2 are decision rules over confidence intervals rather than tests with a single statistic, each is judged by its interval conditions. Exact McNemar P values are corrected across benchmarks within each arm by Holm’s method11. A hypothesis whose cells are incomplete at the data cutoff is reported as undetermined. Differences are reported in each benchmark’s own metric. H3 (which decision point carries the effect) is exploratory, as are all results on protocolqa2 and OmicsBench and all comparisons not named in the hypotheses. A single-round arm whose primary lower bound lies between zero and the margin receives a second round, and the two rounds are judged together, an adaptive design. Intervals resample tasks, and between-round variation of the baseline enters through σb\sigma_{b}. On SeqQA and seqqa2, later baseline rounds ran at a lower host load than the arms, so wall-clock changes there are paired with baseline round 1, which ran in the same period; scores and steps use all reference rounds. At the data cutoff, arms are paired on the tasks graded in the baseline reference and in every arm of the benchmark, a benchmark enters H1 only if these cover at least max(30, N/2) of its N tasks, and σb\sigma_{b} may use the completed part of a paused baseline round with at least 30 tasks. The motivating trajectories used agent commit 1da1a4a and two earlier skill releases (45 and 83 skills).

Panel coverage

For a set 𝒯\mathcal{T} of targets gg and a probe set PP with footprints fp⁡(p)\mathrm{fp}(p), mean per-target design and post-screen coverage and the fully covered fraction are

Cdesign=1|𝒯|​∑g∈𝒯|bases⁡(g)∩⋃p∈Pfp⁡(p)||bases⁡(g)|,Cscreen=1|𝒯|​∑g∈𝒯|bases⁡(g)∩⋃p∈Ppassfp⁡(p)||bases⁡(g)|,Fscreen=|{g∈𝒯:bases⁡(g)⊆⋃p∈Ppassfp⁡(p)}||𝒯|,\begin{gathered}C_{\text{design}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum_{g\in\mathcal{T}}\frac{\bigl|\mathrm{bases}(g)\cap\bigcup_{p\in P}\mathrm{fp}(p)\bigr|}{|\mathrm{bases}(g)|},\\ C_{\text{screen}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum_{g\in\mathcal{T}}\frac{\bigl|\mathrm{bases}(g)\cap\bigcup_{p\in P_{\text{pass}}}\mathrm{fp}(p)\bigr|}{|\mathrm{bases}(g)|},\\ F_{\text{screen}}=\frac{\bigl|\{g\in\mathcal{T}:\mathrm{bases}(g)\subseteq\bigcup_{p\in P_{\text{pass}}}\mathrm{fp}(p)\}\bigr|}{|\mathcal{T}|},\end{gathered} (17)

where Ppass⊆PP_{\text{pass}}\subseteq P are the probes that pass genome-wide specificity screening. For the default design Cdesign=0.884C_{\text{design}}=0.884, Cscreen=0.158C_{\text{screen}}=0.158 and Fscreen=16/123F_{\text{screen}}=16/123; for the 70-nt design Cdesign=1.0C_{\text{design}}=1.0, Cscreen=0.204C_{\text{screen}}=0.204 and Fscreen=21/123F_{\text{screen}}=21/123. Restricted to the 41 targets outside C4A/C4B, Cdesign=0.712C_{\text{design}}=0.712 and Cscreen=0.475C_{\text{screen}}=0.475 (default) and 1.01.0 and 0.6120.612 (70 nt). The 70-nt design also widens the GC window from 0.30–0.70 to 0.20–0.85 and relaxes the hairpin, dimer and background-hit limits.

Probe-design tools

Probes were tiled with MrBait v1.2.7. Specificity was screened genome-wide on GRCh37 with BWA-MEM v0.7.19 and BLAST 2.16.0 under fixed specificity thresholds, and coverage computed with bedtools v2.31.112 and mosdepth13. Capture libraries were processed with fastp14, BWA-MEM (v0.7.17), Picard MarkDuplicates15 and bamdst16 against targets padded by 60 bp; uniformity is the fraction of target bases with depth at least 0.2 times the sample’s mean depth. Melting temperature, hairpin and self-dimer checks used nearest-neighbour thermodynamics69. Per-probe keep-or-redesign decisions were split by target group into training, development and test sets of 2,818, 827 and 591 records, and the held-out evaluation set is a labelled slice of the test groups with 150 binary decisions (25 targets, 75 of each label). The label is the outcome of the genome-wide specificity screen for the probe. The hosted decision model answered each decision zero-shot as a closed two-option question, and the public LAYA checkpoint was scored on the same set.

Compute

All runs used CPUs only, on a shared 96-core, 182-GB host without GPUs, inside a dedicated control group capped at 90 cores and 160 GB without swap, with separate allocations for benchmark items, controller serving and training. Per-task core budgets were 1 (SeqQA, seqqa2), 2 (BixBench-Verified-50, BiomniBench-DA, protocolqa2) and 4 (SciAgentArena, OmicsBench). Baseline rounds and controller arms ran concurrently on the same host, and absolute wall-clock times depend on its load. Slow-system and judge costs were taken from provider usage and a fixed price table.

Extended Data Fig. 1 || Errors after the computation in the formal evaluation. a, Failure classes of wrong baseline answers by rule codebook, per benchmark (wrong/total: SeqQA 11/600, seqqa2 23/400, BixBench-Verified-50 6/50, SciAgentArena 81/189, BiomniBench-DA 38/50 below full marks, protocolqa2 32/125, OmicsBench 2/3). Convention errors are detectable only on benchmarks with answer matchers (SeqQA, seqqa2 and BixBench-Verified-50). b, Share of wrong answers with an answer matcher whose correct value had appeared in the agent’s own tool output, per arm, with Wilson 95% intervals. c, Post-answer share of all wall-clock time, a lower bound on ω\omega, per arm and benchmark, with 95% cluster-bootstrap intervals.

Extended Data Fig. 2 || Speed and cost including the controller. a, Time per controller request at four decision points of the formal evaluation (Table 1), for LAYA version 0 on CPU, JEV and the general-LLM controller. Dots are medians and lines extend to the 95th percentile. Points with fewer than 30 requests are omitted. The shaded band is the range of the median slow-system step across benchmarks, computed as wall-clock time minus controller time, divided by agent steps, over the baseline rounds of the main table. b, Controller share of wall-clock time per benchmark for JEV, LAYA version 0 and the general-LLM controller, with 95% intervals. c, Controller share of cost per task for JEV and the general-LLM controller. The brief is not shown. LAYA runs locally with no per-request price.

Extended Data Fig. 3 || Calibration and selective prediction. a, Reliability diagrams of JEV and the general-LLM controller on benchmark states, for the error class (labels from the failing call’s output), the analysis family and the answer type (labels from the benchmark). Bins of 0.1 in stated confidence with at least five decisions are shown, and each panel gives the expected calibration error. b, Accuracy of answered error-triage questions against coverage as the action threshold varies. Dots mark the threshold of 0.6 used in the evaluation.

Extended Data Fig. 4 || Where the controller helps. Paired score change against the baseline by difficulty stratum (pass rate over the other controller arms) (a), by tertile of trajectory length in agent steps (b) and per seqqa2 task family, 15–20 tasks per family (c). Strata with fewer than ten tasks are not shown. Error bars, 95% cluster-bootstrap intervals, clipped at the axis limits.

Extended Data Fig. 5 || Skill release and controller effect. a, Controller effect on score (arm minus baseline) in the earlier run (hollow) and in the main run (filled), per benchmark and arm (paired tasks: SeqQA 594, seqqa2 386, BixBench-Verified-50 49, SciAgentArena 158). The two runs differ in skill release and in the agent’s reasoning effort. For protocolqa2 (124 tasks) the comparison is skill release r03 against r04b at the same effort, and the two series also differ in frozen code and run time. The general-LLM arm did not run in the earlier run, and BiomniBench-DA is omitted (16 paired tasks). b, The same comparison per seqqa2 validator family (15–20 tasks per family).
